name: Career Transition

claims.claim_text: Engineers who dislike their current area of electronics commonly ask whether taking a further course of study will open a route out; the answer given from long exposure to that question on the EEVblog forum is that additional study is not the mechanism, and that the move is made by changing jobs directly.
claims.quote_verbatim: Just get out and go and get another job.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: China, Entrepreneurs and Blue Collar Reality

claims.claim_text: Publishing tutorials publicly while learning a subject builds visible credibility for someone whose formal study lies elsewhere, because the record shows the learning process itself and is useful to other people; it is one route by which a person studying an unrelated field establishes standing in electronics.
claims.quote_verbatim: he started a site and he started doing tutorials as he went along, you know, and, and that's given him credibility
claims.episode_title: China, Entrepreneurs and Blue Collar Reality

claims.claim_text: Being transferred onto a product line that a newer product from the same company has already displaced is a signal that the role is ending: Philip Frieden worked on AMD's 29000 family and was then made the last product planning manager for the 2900 bit-slice line that the 29000 had superseded.
claims.quote_verbatim: the writing was on the wall, although I refused to read it. And that was the 29,000 that I'd worked on was pretty much the death knell for 2900
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: The Art of Electronics works poorly as a first textbook but well as a refresher for an engineer returning to design work after time away; a concentrated read of a couple of weeks was enough preparation to be hired back into design after a period out of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: That's how I recapped all of my knowledge and got hired for a job. It was like, I was out of design for a while. I just started reading Art of Electronics for like a couple weeks straight.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: A common trigger for leaving a large semiconductor employer to found a company is reaching the limit of what can be achieved inside it rather than dissatisfaction with the employer: Brett Fox left Maxim, about which he stated he had nothing but good things to say, once the choice narrowed to continuing in the same role or attempting something different.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was at a time, personally, where I was seeing the end of the line for me in terms of what I could achieve at Maxim
claims.speaker: Brett Fox
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Brett Fox and Dr Jeroen Fonderie - Device Doubling Decretum

claims.claim_text: During the dot-com and IT boom, vendor networking certifications such as Microsoft's and Cisco's were, by one recollection offered with the qualifier that the figure may be exaggerated, worth on the order of a $200,000 salary, which drew people into the field on the strength of the credential alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you got one of those, right, you were guaranteed a $200,000 a year job at the time.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hardware, Surveys and Giveaways - Radular Rental Ranting

claims.claim_text: When the IT market collapsed, the people who had switched careers on the strength of a certification found the credential no longer commanded a premium, with some unable to obtain work at a fifth of the salary the boom had promised. A career change timed to a hiring boom carries the risk that the boom, not the skill, was the thing being paid for.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's all these people going, I switched my career for this. And now I can't even get a $40,000 a year job
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Hardware, Surveys and Giveaways - Radular Rental Ranting

claims.claim_text: Entering paid embedded work without an engineering degree is possible where a sustained compulsion to build supplies the skill; the distinguishing feature is that the work is what the person would be doing anyway rather than a hobby that is switched off when the paid day ends.
claims.quote_verbatim: the whole reason why I have an English degree and can be in there, like getting hired to do this stuff is because of, of this, this bug
claims.speaker: Todd Bailey
claims.episode_title: An Interview With Todd Bailey - Embedded Embrasure Engineering

claims.claim_text: The early-1990s recession pushed electronics students into computing and IT, a redirection common enough at the time that leaving an electronics course part-way through for an IT career was unremarkable; that IT career then ran twenty years.
claims.quote_verbatim: I didn't finish my electronics at college because I realized it was in the early 90s and there was a bit of a recession. So, I decided at that point in time I wanted to go into computers and IT.
claims.speaker: Martin Lorton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Martin Lorton - Variegated Video Vagility

claims.claim_text: An international relocation driven by a partner's employment need not end the other partner's career: continuing the existing job by telecommuting across the move preserved employment through a two-year posting abroad, in this case through the period in which EDS was bought by HP.
claims.quote_verbatim: So, we ended up here in the States because my wife works for an accounting company. And so, they brought her over here on the comment. I came along, but I telecommuted. I continued my job for EDS slash HP.
claims.speaker: Martin Lorton
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Martin Lorton - Variegated Video Vagility

claims.claim_text: Where a business is to be founded can be chosen deliberately rather than inherited: after eleven months of travel spent evaluating locations, Seattle was selected as a base, on the judgment that starting a business in the United States is easier and more advisable than doing so elsewhere.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's a lot easier and advisable if you can to start a business in the U.S. than elsewhere.
claims.speaker: Fabienne Serriere
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Fabienne Serrière of KnitYak

claims.claim_text: Two product businesses in unrelated markets cannot be run at once by one person; the transition between them was planned as a staged wind-down of one over roughly a year while the other was returned to production and its line expanded.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's going to mean a transition for me because I'm going to get out of the fashion world and get back in the music business because I can't do both
claims.speaker: Fran Blanche
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: The move to full-time independent electronics content was not a planned career change but the consequence of redundancy: being laid off by Altium was the event that converted a part-time blog into a full-time occupation.
claims.quote_verbatim: That, yeah, made me go full time.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Catalyzing Change Agents

claims.claim_text: A stated reason for leaving a settled engineering job is the expectation of stopping learning if the stay continues; in this case that judgment coincided with family reasons for returning to Slovakia, and the departure was made without a new engineering job lined up, the initial plan being to write websites instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: Actually, I wanted to do some change because I felt like I'm not going to grow. And I felt like if I stay longer, I may become the lazy person, which is not going to, you know, learn anything new.
claims.speaker: Robert Feranec
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Robert Feranec

claims.claim_text: One model for a long technical career is a sequence of self-directed programmes of roughly four to five years each in a new domain, run using the method for learning a field acquired during a doctorate; successive cycles covered chip design, optics, and manufacturing and electronics.
claims.quote_verbatim: I did another sort of same-style kind of program around another topic that took about four to five years. And that was like in chip design.
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: The barrier to moving into a genuinely unrelated technical field is logistical rather than intellectual: a newcomer cannot bill at a serious level in the new field, so the transition has to be funded from somewhere other than the new work.
claims.quote_verbatim: I am such a noob there that I can't even pay the bills in any serious sense doing any real biology work
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bunnie Huang (2nd)

claims.claim_text: A request to reduce to part-time hours is a negotiation an employer can simply refuse; where the employer has no part-time arrangement to offer, the request can end in a full departure rather than a reduced one.
claims.quote_verbatim: I asked to go part time. Right. Where, where, and they said, we don't do that
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: All the way with DLJ

claims.claim_text: The largest adjustment in turning long-running unpaid project work into a livelihood is that each activity must afterwards be justified by the income it produces rather than chosen for interest alone.
claims.quote_verbatim: I've been doing this because I wanted to and for the fun of it. And now I need to justify doing things because I need the income.
claims.speaker: Jon Oxer
claims.episode_title: An(other) Interview with Jon Oxer

claims.claim_text: In the wind-down of a startup, the terms an engineer can obtain depend on holding something of value; without leverage the outcome is dictated to them, and securing an asset of value shifts the balance of the negotiation.
claims.quote_verbatim: If you have no leverage, you're going to get screwed over. If you have something of value, which we somehow managed to get something of value, then it flipped the power a little bit.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: An engineer with a public specialism in a field large companies are entering does not have to search for work after a startup fails; where the specialism was augmented reality, senior positions were offered by the major companies unprompted.
claims.quote_verbatim: So I had all the big players like, oh, my God, we're doing augmented reality. You do augmented reality. We have a senior position for you.
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: Jeri Ellsworth and the demise of CastAR

claims.claim_text: Professional orchestral employment is structurally scarce because a post only opens when an incumbent leaves and is then filled by audition, which is a standing reason musicians move into technical work.
claims.quote_verbatim: in the orchestra world, it's like somebody has to leave a position and then there's an audition
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: One route out of a first career is to build income in the destination field part-time alongside it: part-time writing for Hackaday and private teaching supplemented a musician's income, and the option to go full-time arrived when Supply Frame bought the site in 2013.
claims.quote_verbatim: But I started, you know, writing part-time for Hackaday as a way to kind of round out my income.
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: A skill set abandoned at the start of a technical career can become the basis of a later one: two years of college aimed at theatre lighting design gave way to online software work during the dot-com boom, and the performance and storytelling side lay unused for about ten years until video distribution existed to make use of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I still always had that sort of, you know, passion for, I guess, storytelling and, and performance and, and, um, and that had sort of, you know, like dormant, um, for, for 10 years.
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Scotty Allen (Strangeparts)

claims.claim_text: Hardware employment is geographically concentrated, and the Seattle area in particular held a substantial number of hardware openings and employers, which is a consideration for anyone timing a return to electronics work.
claims.quote_verbatim: And in the Seattle area, hardware is big. There's a lot of opportunities in Seattle for hardware.
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer
claims.episode_title: The Legend of Keyzermas

claims.claim_text: For a consultant, unpaid skill-building during a slack period can convert directly into billable work: self-directed study of robotics and machine learning, covering the Robot Operating System, image processing and deep neural networks, was followed by a contract that used all of it.
claims.quote_verbatim: I did a bunch of work on it on my own. Cause I had some free time. And then suddenly I had a contract that was using every single bit of it.
claims.speaker: Elecia White
claims.episode_title: Stick 'Em On Whales

claims.claim_text: The sale of an employer to a competitor functions as a decision point rather than an automatic transfer, and having a standing offer elsewhere at that moment is what makes the exit available; in this case the standing offer led to joining Inventables.
claims.quote_verbatim: the company I was working for was going through a sale to a competitor. I wasn't really that interested in moving, you know, working for this competitor. And I had this open offer from Zach.
claims.speaker: Bart Dring
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: A public open-source project can generate the contact that later becomes a job: a company searching for the leading open-source laser cutter found its author working a few miles away, and the relationship that began with sample kits and gift certificates preceded the eventual offer of employment.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was looking for, you know, the number one open source laser out there and was surprised to find, you know, it's just two, three miles from our office
claims.speaker: Bart Dring
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Bart Dring

claims.claim_text: Winding down a training and consulting business need not be a single retirement event: at 60 the expectation was never to retire, by about 65 fatigue prompted a cut to fewer hours per week and to roughly one seminar trip per month, and at just short of 67 retirement was still not intended.
claims.quote_verbatim: And so I cut back to fewer hours per week and cut back to just one trip, typically a trip to do a seminar a month.
claims.speaker: Jack Ganssle
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jack Ganssle (2nd)

claims.claim_text: Founding a company can require leaving a job that is not itself the problem; the stated reason for quitting a job she liked, with limited savings, was that the attempt would otherwise never be made.
claims.quote_verbatim: I quit my job, even though I loved my job and I thought it was great, but I was like, if I don't do this now, I'm never going to do it. So I quit my job. I didn't have a ton of savings, but I had enough to just kind of start coding.
claims.speaker: Natasha Baker
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: An engineer founding a software product usually can acquire the missing skills, so the binding constraint is not capability but runway: whether there is enough saved time and money to spend learning them before the product must earn.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can, you can figure it out over enough time, but do you want to spend that time and you have the runway to do that sort of thing?
claims.episode_title: Footprints and Symbols with Natasha Baker

claims.claim_text: Leaving a stable salary to work independently rests on preconditions that are assembled beforehand: a support network and accumulated savings from a well-paid job made the departure survivable.
claims.quote_verbatim: I had a support network. Of course I had, I had a good job. I was able to save, you know, I'm a long time saver.
claims.speaker: Shrouk El Attar
claims.episode_title: Creative Engineering with Shrouk El-Attar

claims.claim_text: Someone with dependants moving into an unproven income source treats risk reduction as the governing constraint; in this case it took about four years of running a channel alongside a job before the shift was judged feasible at all.
claims.quote_verbatim: But as an older guy getting into YouTube, I didn't want to risk, right?
claims.speaker: Mehdi Sadaghdar
claims.episode_title: Electroboom!

claims.claim_text: A staged transition from salaried work to independent media income can be indexed to income thresholds: when Patreon plus channel revenue reached half the salary, the salaried role was cut to part-time, and about six months later, once the revenue matched the whole salary, the job was left entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: that plus the income from the YouTube can cover half of my income. Oh, okay. Right. So, I thought to myself, okay, let's make myself part-time. I made myself part-time. Right. And then, I don't know, like, six months after, I realized that, hey, I can cover my entire salary.
claims.speaker: Mehdi Sadaghdar
claims.episode_title: Electroboom!

claims.claim_text: Employer mandates returning staff to the office became a reason to change jobs for those who valued remote work, and the value placed on it divides by household circumstances: one engineer was ready to return after six months at home, while people with children weighed it very differently. The related trade is accepting a less enjoyable job for higher pay when the enjoyable one does not cover the bills.
claims.quote_verbatim: some places are going or moving back to everyone in office and people really enjoyed the work from home, which for me, I got really after six months of working from home, I was ready to go back to the office. But for some people that have family kids, you know, which totally makes sense actually from working from home.
claims.speaker: Parker Dillman
claims.episode_title: Pavlovian Cheapskates

claims.claim_text: Corporate restructuring can relocate an engineer internationally instead of ending the job: in Altium's reorganisation around 2011 staff were either moved to Shanghai or laid off, while one employee was instead moved back to the United States.
claims.quote_verbatim: when Altium moved everyone else to Shanghai or laid people off, I got moved back to the U.S.
claims.speaker: Ben Jordan
claims.episode_title: Publicly Traded Hobby with Ben Jordan

claims.claim_text: Success in leading a growing company removes the founder from the technical work that started it: Ray Ozzie, a developer by background, stopped coding in 1996 as the company he led grew, the work shifting to managing people.
claims.quote_verbatim: I was a developer and I, because of success, because of leading a company that was getting larger and larger, I had to stop coding in 96
claims.speaker: Ray Ozzie
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ray Ozzie (Blues Wireless)

claims.claim_text: Converting a skill practised as a side project into a job description removes the option of abandoning the parts that are hard or unenjoyable, and adds schedule pressure that the same work did not carry when it was voluntary.
claims.quote_verbatim: when you're doing it as like a passion hobby project, if you get to something that's really hard that you don't like, you can just be like, ah, whatever
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys
claims.episode_title: Building Firmware and Hardware for Trade Shows with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: Developer-relations work at a small company resembles consulting in its day-to-day shape: internal and external customers, frequent context switching, and integration of existing platforms and libraries rather than building base-level technology such as network drivers, which is what makes it a workable destination for someone moving from content work into firmware.
claims.quote_verbatim: it does kind of feel like kind of, kind of like consulting, right? It's kind of like, uh, you know, we have a bunch of internal customers sort of thing, maybe some external customers, but it is a lot of like changing, a lot of of context switching pretty often
claims.speaker: Mike Szczys
claims.episode_title: Building Firmware and Hardware for Trade Shows with Mike Szczys

claims.claim_text: Electrical engineering graduates of around 2000 entered a market that had just collapsed and many moved into IT instead, a path common enough to recur repeatedly among students later returning to electronics training.
claims.quote_verbatim: I, I went to school for electrical engineering. It was like, the money was supposed to be so good in that. And then like, you know, I graduated in 2000 and like the bottom fell out, you know, there was nothing there. And so then I went into IT eventually.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Gremlins in the machine

claims.claim_text: Where a target speciality has few openings and heavy competition, one route in is to create the position rather than apply for it: unable to find an audio electronics job from a role in oil and gas, one engineer left and ran his own audio electronics business for several years instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: getting into audio electronics is incredibly difficult because it's just super competitive and there's not a lot of opportunities out there. So I said, you know what, I I'll just do it. I'll just make it happen. So I left, I left that company in the first place and started my own business doing audio electronics.
claims.speaker: Stephen Craig
claims.episode_title: Engineering Careers with Circuit Break & James Lewis

claims.claim_text: A first job that turns out to be field technician work rather than the design work trained for is a reason to move rather than to wait for internal promotion; an unwillingness to wait two years for the intended work led to a move found through an industry job board in the 2011 to 2012 period.
claims.quote_verbatim: I wanted to do actual engineering work. I didn't want to be a technician out in the field and I wasn't going to wait two years to do that.
claims.episode_title: Engineering Careers with Circuit Break & James Lewis

claims.claim_text: Career planning by job title tends to be abandoned with experience: after roughly ten years and several job changes the target shifts from a named position to a broader description of the work, and repeated changes reduce the reluctance to make drastic ones later.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was probably after about 10 years that I stopped having that as my, my, my end point or my plan. It was, I wanted to kind of, my, my plan became much more broader than this specific position
claims.episode_title: Engineering Careers with Circuit Break & James Lewis

claims.claim_text: For an engineer moving back into design from an adjacent non-design role such as operations management, the binding difficulty is obtaining the first opportunity rather than the technical knowledge, since remaining at an engineering company keeps the person partly in touch with the work.
claims.quote_verbatim: this is basically a big career shift, right? And I think the hard thing is just going to be getting a shot
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Turtles as a Service

claims.claim_text: Electrical installation is a licensed trade with protected entry, so a mid-career change into it requires serving a full apprenticeship regardless of the entrant's age or prior career.
claims.quote_verbatim: yeah, but no, it's a fully protected industry. So I got a friend who's in his forties and he decided to go back and become an electrician.
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Troubleshooting is the skill

claims.claim_text: Reducing fixed living costs is one way to make a modest independent income sufficient: moving from Boston to Pittsburgh brought a mortgage to a little over $500 a month, at which point existing Patreon support was enough to leave a staff job at Formlabs and work on the project full-time.
claims.quote_verbatim: Pittsburgh is way cheaper to live in than Boston, which is where Formlabs was. And I was making like just my mortgage is was like, oh man, it was like a little over $500.
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

claims.claim_text: An offer of venture funding is not automatically the right next step for a newly independent hardware project: an approach from a patron offering venture capital was declined because taking it was understood to mean closing the source, against the intent of keeping the design a common good.
claims.quote_verbatim: I told him to pound sand because I was not interested in like making it go close source.
claims.speaker: Stephen Hawes
claims.episode_title: A Benchtop Pick and Place with Stephen Hawes

attribution_notes: Episode 14: bundle labels the passage Chris Gammell; the advice about people asking on 'my forum' whether another course is a route out is content-identified as Dave Jones (EEVblog forum), so that claim is attributed to him. The Tronixstuff tutorial-site remarks in the same fused passage cannot be assigned between the two voices, so that claim uses speaker null.
Episode 93 (Tom LeMense) passage was read and dropped: personal narrative with no transferable content.
Episode 190: 'screw you money' line is an interjection in a fused two-voice passage and cannot be assigned to either host from content; speaker null.

Episode 194: bundle marks attribution unreliable and the passage is the guest's own account of holding an English degree while being hired for embedded work, so attributed to Todd Bailey, the interviewee.

Episode 206: bundle marks attribution unreliable; the two claims kept are the guest's own career account and are attributed to Martin Lorton. The separate passage in which the speaker describes long hours and good pay from full-time video was declined and dropped, because content shows the first half of that passage is the host answering before Martin is asked the same question.
Episode 257: bundle marks attribution unreliable; the passage is the guest describing her own relocation and business, so attributed to Fabienne Serriere.

Episode 306: bundle labels the passage Chris Gammell, but the line 'made me go full time' answers Chris's question about the Altium redundancy and is Dave Jones speaking about himself; attributed to Dave Jones.

Episode 336: the Bunnie Huang claims are taken from the passage labelled Bunnie Huang rather than the near-identical passage labelled Dave Jones, which contains the same material as the earlier speaker's question.
Episode 341: bundle marks attribution unreliable and labels the passage Dave Jones; the account of asking to go part-time at ABB is Chris Gammell's own employment, so attributed to Chris Gammell.

Episode 394: bundle labels the passage Chris Gammell; the leverage remark uses 'we' for the CastAR side and immediately precedes Chris addressing the guest by name, and the account of being approached with senior augmented-reality positions is the guest's own, so both are attributed to Jeri Ellsworth.
Episode 438: bundle marks attribution unreliable; the account of an employer being sold and of an open-source laser project leading to Inventables is the guest's own, so attributed to Bart Dring.

Episode 531: bundle marks attribution unreliable; the account of quitting to build the product is the guest's own and is attributed to Natasha Baker. The runway remark in the same passage is phrased as a question from the interviewer and is left at speaker null.

Episode 593: bundle marks attribution unreliable and labels the passage Dave Jones; the speaker describing leaving Autodesk and being moved back to the United States when Altium restructured is the guest, Ben Jordan.
Episode 622: bundle labels the passage Dave Jones, but the firmware-versus-side-project and developer-relations material is the guest describing his own move, so attributed to Mike Szczys.

Episode 625: two voices; only the account of students who graduated in 2000 and moved into IT, which refers to sign-ups for the speaker's own course, is kept, and it is attributed to Chris Gammell. The adjacent warning about over-focusing on one hot skill is speculative about the future and was dropped.

Episode 670: the audio electronics business account is attributed to Stephen Craig as labelled; the separate account of refusing to wait two years in a field technician role occurs after a speaker change within the same fused passage and could not be assigned, so it uses speaker null. The five-year-plan passage is labelled Dave Jones, but the ten-year remark addresses Steven by name and belongs to another participant, so it is left null.
Three passages carry a null episode and were dropped as uncitable.
